deck.name: Databases
deck.description: Реляционные базы данных и работа с ними

cards.definition_en: A request to a database to read or change data, written in a language such as SQL.
examples: The query returned all orders from the last week.
A slow query kept the whole page waiting.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it like 'queue-ry'.
Using 'request' and 'query' as the same thing: a query concerns the data store.

cards.definition_en: A separate structure that helps the database find rows quickly without reading the whole table.
examples: Adding an index on the email column made the search instant.
Every index speeds up reading but slows down writing a little.
common_mistakes: Adding an index on every column.
Believing an index is free: it uses disk space and slows down writes.

cards.definition_en: A group of database operations that are treated as one unit: either all of them succeed or none of them take effect.
examples: The transfer runs in one transaction, so money never disappears halfway.
A transaction that stays open too long can block other users.
common_mistakes: Using 'transaction' only for payments.
Forgetting to end the transaction after an error.

cards.definition_en: A set of four properties - atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability - that describe reliable database transactions.
examples: The bank requires a database with ACID guarantees.
Durability, the D in ACID, means committed data survives a crash.
common_mistakes: Reading the A as 'accuracy': it stands for atomicity.
Thinking every database provides ACID in every mode.

cards.definition_en: A column or set of columns whose value is unique for every row and identifies that row.
examples: The user table uses the id column as its primary key.
Two rows cannot have the same primary key.
common_mistakes: Allowing empty values in a primary key.
Using a value that changes, such as a phone number, as a primary key.

cards.definition_en: A column that points to the primary key of another table and so links the rows of two tables.
examples: The orders table has a foreign key pointing to the customers table.
The database refused the insert because the foreign key did not match any customer.
common_mistakes: Thinking a foreign key comes from another database.
Mixing it up with a primary key.

cards.definition_en: The description of how a database is organized: its tables, columns, types and relations.
examples: The team reviewed the schema before adding the new table.
A change in the schema must be applied to every environment.
common_mistakes: Writing 'scheme' for the database term.
Changing the schema by hand on production.

cards.definition_en: Organizing tables so that each fact is stored in only one place, which avoids repeated and contradictory data.
examples: After normalization the customer address is stored once and not in every order.
Too much normalization can make queries need many joins.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with the normalizing of text or numbers.
Thinking it always makes queries faster.

cards.definition_en: Deliberately storing some data in more than one place to make reading faster, accepting extra work to keep copies consistent.
examples: Denormalization saved the report from joining five tables.
Each denormalization adds a risk that copies disagree.
common_mistakes: Treating it as a mistake in every case.
Doing it before measuring a real performance problem.

cards.definition_en: An operation that combines rows from two or more tables according to a related column.
examples: The query uses a join to show each order with the customer's name.
A missing join condition produced millions of rows.
common_mistakes: Forgetting the join condition.
Mixing up the left join and the inner join.

cards.definition_en: A named set of commands saved inside the database that applications can run with one call.
examples: The application calls a stored procedure to close the month.
Putting a lot of logic into a stored procedure makes testing harder.
common_mistakes: Thinking it is stored outside the database.
Building the call by joining text with user input.

cards.definition_en: Automatically copying data from one database server to others so that copies stay in sync.
examples: Replication keeps a second server ready in case the first one fails.
Replication lag made the replica show old data for a few seconds.
common_mistakes: Treating replication as a backup: a mistaken deletion is copied too.
Reading from a replica and expecting the very latest write.

cards.definition_en: Splitting a large database into parts, each stored on a different server, according to some rule such as the user's identifier.
examples: Sharding spreads the users across ten servers.
A poor sharding key sends most traffic to one server.
common_mistakes: Mixing it up with replication, which copies the same data.
Choosing a sharding key that changes over time.

cards.definition_en: A situation in which two transactions each wait for a resource held by the other, so neither can continue.
examples: The database canceled one transaction to break the deadlock.
Updating tables in the same order reduces the chance of a deadlock.
common_mistakes: Treating a deadlock as a crash of the server.
Retrying the transaction without changing its order.

cards.definition_en: A setting that decides how much one running transaction can see of the changes made by others.
examples: A higher isolation level gives safer results but allows less parallel work.
The report ran with a lower isolation level and saw changes from other transactions.
common_mistakes: Raising the isolation level for every query without a reason.
Thinking all databases use the same default.

cards.definition_en: A versioned script that changes the structure of a database from one state to the next, so every environment can be updated the same way.
examples: The deployment runs the migration before starting the new version.
A migration that locks a big table can stop the service.
common_mistakes: Editing an old migration after it was applied elsewhere.
Using 'migration' for moving to another provider only.

cards.definition_en: A saved query that behaves like a virtual table.
examples: The reporting view hides the columns with personal data.
A materialized view stores the result and must be refreshed.
common_mistakes: Thinking an ordinary view stores a copy of the data.
Confusing the database term with the view in an interface.

cards.definition_en: Code stored in the database that runs automatically when a certain change happens in a table.
examples: A trigger writes a record to the audit table whenever a salary is changed.
Hidden triggers can surprise developers who do not know they exist.
common_mistakes: Mixing it up with a stored procedure, which has to be called explicitly.
Putting heavy logic into a trigger.

cards.definition_en: A rule enforced by the database, such as a value being unique, not empty or within a range.
examples: A unique constraint on the email column prevents duplicate accounts.
The insert failed because it violated a constraint.
common_mistakes: Relying only on the application to check rules.
Disabling constraints to speed up an import and forgetting to enable them.

cards.definition_en: A set of ready database connections that an application reuses instead of opening a new one for every request.
examples: The connection pool has twenty connections shared by all requests.
Slow queries can exhaust the connection pool.
common_mistakes: Opening a new connection for each request.
Setting the pool larger than the database allows.

cards.definition_en: A technique that lets a program work with database rows as objects, hiding most of the SQL.
examples: Object-relational mapping saves time on simple queries.
The object-relational mapping produced hundreds of queries for one page.
common_mistakes: Expecting it to remove the need to understand SQL.
Ignoring the queries that the tool generates.

cards.definition_en: A group of databases that do not use tables and the SQL language in the traditional way, such as document or key-value stores.
examples: The team chose a NoSQL database for flexible documents.
Many NoSQL systems trade strict consistency for scalability.
common_mistakes: Reading it as 'no SQL' meaning that SQL is forbidden: it is often read as 'not only SQL'.
Assuming it is always faster than a relational database.

cards.definition_en: The step-by-step strategy the database chooses to carry out a query, which can be inspected to understand why it is slow.
examples: The execution plan showed a full table scan instead of using the index.
Developers read the execution plan before rewriting a slow query.
common_mistakes: Guessing why a query is slow without reading the plan.
Confusing the plan with the result of the query.

cards.definition_en: The step that makes all the changes of a transaction permanent and visible to others.
examples: The changes become permanent only after the commit.
A crash before the commit leaves the data as it was.
common_mistakes: Confusing a database commit with a commit in version control.
Calling commit before all the operations are finished.

cards.definition_en: A frozen copy of the state of a database or disk at one moment in time.
examples: A snapshot of the volume was taken before the upgrade.
Restoring the snapshot returned the database to yesterday's state.
common_mistakes: Confusing a snapshot with replication, which keeps copying changes continuously.
Writing 'snap shot' as two words.
